newsitem.title: ERITREA: Sudan rebels say they capture southern town.
newsitem.headline: Sudan rebels say they capture southern town.

text.p: The Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA) said on Friday a joint rebel force had captured the town of Maban on the southern front of the Blue Nile region as the government poured in forces to counter the rebel advance.

Yassir Arman, spokesman for John Garang, head of the SPLA and chairman of a joint military command, told Reuters rebels were now marching towards Damazin, where a hydro-electric station supplies the Sudanese capital of Khartoum with most of its power.
There was no independent confirmation of Arman's claim.
Arman said 980 members of the government army militia had surrendered and joined rebel ranks.

The rebels say they have already seized two towns on the border with Ethiopia -- Kurmuk and Qeissan, about 600-km (370-miles) southeast of Khartoum -- and on Monday they said they captured key army garrisons at Al-Kali, Daimonsour and Shali al-Fil in the southern Blue Nile region.
"Yesterday (Thursday) our joint forces captured Maban town which is south of Kurmuk. They captured the town without fighting," Arman said in the Eritrean capital of Asmara.
"The NIF (government) forces fled because they are in low morale after the defeat of the other forces in the area and they see no hope for reinforcement from Khartoum," said Arman.
Arman said Maban was a strategic bypass for the White Nile state, Upper Nile and the Blue Nile region.
The rebel spokesman said rebel forces were now advancing towards Damazin, a strategic town, which supplies the capital with 80 percent of its power.
"After the fall of Maban, the area south, northeast and west of Kurmuk is all secured. The whole SPLA force in the area is advancing towards Damazin after clearing their rear."

The rebels have ruled out an advance on Khartoum but they say they want to pile on economic and military pressure to trigger an uprising against the government of military ruler Omar Hassan al-Bashir.
Arman said Garang has appealed to government soldiers and militia in the southern Sudan to join his forces.
Garang's SPLA has been fighting in southern Sudan since 1983 but the rebel movement suffered setbacks when it splintered in 1991.
It has since recovered, thanks to a military and political alliance with northern opposition groups based in Eritrea.
Sudan has accused Ethiopia and Eritrea of invading its territory and coordinating the rebel attacks. Both countries have denied involvement.
The Sudanese military ruler has called for general mobilisation against the threat, including sending university students to the front.
